tPOT Research Centre, Technological University Dublin

tspan.tspan: Background
VideoTimbre is an experimental music synthesizer that facilitates real-time timbre
modulation by mapping pixel data from a live video stream to a wavetable
synthesis buffer. The specific mapping is performed by an arbitrary user-defined
function, allowing the mode of interaction to be easily customised.
As in conventional wavetable synthesis, notes are produced through looped
playback of the wavetable buffer, with playback rate determining the pitch of each
note. However, unlike conventional wavetable synthesis, VideoTimbre uses no
stored waveforms to define instrument sounds. Instead, all waveforms, and hence
timbres, are extracted in real time from the live video stream. Despite containing no
prior information about instrument sounds, the system allows rich, dynamic and
original musical timbres to be created on the fly.
VideoTimbre is fully open. The signal pipeline from video input to audio output is
transparent to the user. The transformation from video pixel data to waveform
buffer samples is user-defined and displayed in the user interface. The codebase is
intentionally minimal (currently ~400 lines) and can be viewed in the browser with a
single mouse click. No third-party libraries or frameworks are used. To permit
unrestricted integration into artists' workflows, VideoTimbre has been placed in the
public domain (Creative Commons CC0).
Implementation
The system is implemented as a purely client-side web application using
JavaScript, HTML5 and CSS. It has minimal dependencies, using the MediaStream
API to access the input video stream, the Web MIDI API to receive MIDI messages
from a connected controller, and the Web Audio API for audio output. The
Chromium browser, which supports all three APIs by default, was used for testing.
The mode of interaction with VideoTimbre depends on the user-defined script that
transforms each video frame into an audio waveform. Several built-in example
scripts are provided. One maps the y-coordinate of the darkest pixel in each column
of pixels to a sample value in the wavetable buffer, allowing a waveform drawn with
a dark pen on white paper to be captured (see image above). Other built-in example
scripts map the maximum or mean pixel value in each column (where each pixel's
value
is defined as the sum of its R, G and B components) to a wavetable buffer
sample. This works well with visual textures that exhibit horizontal variation in
brightness. In each case, users can explore their visual surroundings (e.g. using a
hand-held camera) to discover pleasing timbres.
Exhibition
VideoTimbre was exhibited at Dublin Maker 2026 as an interactive art installation,
Hand-drawn Synth.
Visitors played music on a piano keyboard, while controlling the
timbre of the synthesized notes using a hand-held camera.
